# Hayate Agent Plugins

Plugin adapters for [Hayate Agent](https://github.com/hayate-agent/core): commands,
channels, task delegation, context management and integrations for a persistent
AI assistant.

Optional standalone gateway: [Slack Socket Mode installation](docs/slack-gateway.md)
([app manifest](examples/slack-app-manifest.json)). This local ESM module is
installed explicitly, not fetched or enabled automatically by Core.

**To use Hayate, start with [Core's installation guide](https://github.com/hayate-agent/core#readme).**
Core includes a tested set of plugins. You do not need to install this repository
separately for a normal installation.

## Headless workspace and agent overlay (development)

[Workspace architecture and setup](docs/workspace-architecture.md) describes the
independent `workspace/`, `credentials/`, `git-catalog/`, `identity/` and `agent-hub/` packages.
They own backend state and integrations; the optional WebUI consumes their services.
External agent runtimes are future adapters, not dependencies of the frontend.
This overlay is installed and updated separately from Core. It checks required
host capabilities and service versions; Core need not pin its exact revision or
bundle it.
[Explicit authenticated HTTPS](docs/authenticated-webui.md) protects the API;
[Hayate-to-Hayate HTTPS connectivity](docs/agent-link.md) is implemented as an
optional headless adapter/endpoint; external runtimes remain future adapters.

## Included adapters

- **Task delegation:** dispatcher commands and managed subagents.
- **Context and sessions:** compaction, handover, continuation and session observation.
- **Ongoing work:** loops, cron reports and nightly task strategies.
- **Gateways:** channel registration, routing and activity reporting.
- **[Dashboard API](dashboard-api/README.md):** authenticated HTTP/SSE access to
  conversations and backend services. Contains no browser assets or frontend build.
  The [WebUI](https://github.com/hayate-agent/webui) is a separate project.
- **Review and improvement:** review commands and experiment evaluation adapters.
- **Tools and memory:** memory commands, reloadable tools and optional Wasm tools.

The [manifest](manifest.json) lists the plugin entry points. Core provides the
underlying runtime, persistence, scheduling and policy enforcement.

## How plugins are used

For its existing bundled TypeScript adapters (not the optional overlay), Core
pins a plugin revision and file hashes in `plugins.lock.json`, then
materializes those sources at build time. Published Core checkouts include their
matching sources for offline materialization. Plugin code is not downloaded on
each agent turn.

Plugins are **trusted code with the agent process's permissions**. Review modules
before enabling them. Plugins do not grant permission to bypass tool approvals,
access rules or task boundaries.

## Develop a plugin

Clone this repository alongside a compatible Core checkout:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/hayate-agent/core.git
git clone https://github.com/hayate-agent/plugins.git
```

Follow the [plugin API guide](https://github.com/hayate-agent/core/blob/main/docs/plugins.md)
for commands, tools, channels and lifecycle hooks. Built-in adapters use Core's
TypeScript interfaces; their compatibility gate is Core's typecheck and tests.
For local changes, use Core's materializer with an explicit local source directory
and matching development lock, as described in its
[development guide](https://github.com/hayate-agent/core/blob/main/docs/development.md).

Submit focused pull requests with tests for changed behavior. Never commit
provider credentials, agent identities or deployment-specific configuration.

## Which repository should I use?

| Goal | Project |
| --- | --- |
| Run the agent or use its terminal interface | [Core](https://github.com/hayate-agent/core) |
| Add integrations or backend services | This repository |
| Use the browser dashboard | [WebUI](https://github.com/hayate-agent/webui) |
| Start from deployment examples | [Deployments](https://github.com/hayate-agent/deployments) |

## Related projects

- [Core](https://github.com/hayate-agent/core) — runtime, terminal interface and documentation
- [WebUI](https://github.com/hayate-agent/webui) — independent browser dashboard; consumes the backend API
- [Deployments](https://github.com/hayate-agent/deployments) — deployment examples

## Public snapshot updates

The public repository receives reviewed source snapshots through publishing pull
requests. Changed exports are tested against the public Core before integration;
unchanged snapshots do not require another release. The independent
[WebUI frontend](https://github.com/hayate-agent/webui) remains in its own
repository, while the dashboard API and agent services are maintained here.

## License

[Apache-2.0](LICENSE). This covers the plugin source and backend packages;
Core, WebUI and deployment examples publish their own license files.

# Agent registration

AgentHub owns the registered-agent inventory. It is usable through the dashboard
API or `/agent-hub` commands; it does not require a browser.

## Pair a Hayate target

1. Install credentials, workspace, AgentHub and AgentLink on the target. Enable
   its HTTPS AgentLink listener with a trusted certificate and explicit project
   access policy. The transport configuration is described in `docs/agent-link.md`.
2. On the target, run `/agent-hub pair`. The response contains its enabled endpoint
   and a five-minute, single-use registration code. Generating a code without an
   enabled target endpoint is refused.
3. In the dashboard, open **Agents → Register an agent**. Enter the target endpoint,
   code, display name and optional color. Use the pairing code, not a password.
4. Check the displayed target identity and permissions. **Check connection** sends
   only a scoped read request; it never creates work or replays a message.

The target stores token hashes. The registering instance holds its token in the
credential backend. Neither browser storage nor public agent metadata contains
that token. Codes are stored hashed and consumed atomically. Duplicate endpoint
registration is rejected before consuming a further code.

## Manage a registration

- Rename or recolor an agent without changing its identity, endpoint or credentials.
- Check connectivity; results record their observation time, not a permanent health guarantee.
- Remove an agent by revoking its target authorization first, then removing local credentials and metadata.
- If remote revocation fails, retain the registration for an explicit retry.
- If target revocation succeeded but local cleanup failed, retain that durable state and retry cleanup without using the deleted token.

Adapters without target revocation cannot claim successful removal. Registration
failure after pairing attempts to revoke the newly created authorization. If its
outcome cannot be established, reconcile on the target with `/agent-link list`
and `/agent-link revoke <id>` before pairing again.

Registration establishes connectivity and scoped capabilities. It does not grant
project membership, share files, distribute Git credentials or delete already
accepted work/history when removed.

## Headless management

- `/agent-hub list`
- `/agent-hub check <id>`
- `/agent-hub update {"agentId":"…","patch":{"name":"…","color":"#123456"}}`
- `/agent-hub remove <id>`

All mutations and connection checks participate in the host foreground-work and
shutdown lifecycle. Backend state remains owner-scoped.

# Dashboard API

API-only native gateway for the independently deployed
[Hayate WebUI](https://git.vanillacore.net/harness/webui). This package contains no
HTML, CSS, browser JavaScript, frontend dependencies or browser build.

It owns HTTP/SSE projection of agent-owned conversations and delegates workspace,
identity, credentials and peer operations to their respective backend services.
It does not execute another agent runtime.

## Install

Configure the gateway module as `dashboard-api/index.mjs` in your separately
installed plugin overlay. Keep the existing gateway/channel name `webui`:

```yaml
gatewayPlugins:
  webui:
    module: /absolute/path/to/plugins/dashboard-api/index.mjs
```

The gateway name, host session keys `webui:<id>`, retained
`<agent home>/webui/conversations.json` and configuration files
`webui-network.json` / `webui/ui.json` are stable data/configuration identifiers.
Changing the package directory must not rename them or duplicate existing chats.

The optional settings tool remains an API/backend presentation contract for
operator-controlled declarative settings and trusted module lifecycle; there are
no browser renderers in this package.

## MCP management

With a Core version that provides native MCP user management, type `/mcp` in the
conversation UI. The gateway delivers it as an authenticated channel command;
it is not an agent instruction or a `/v1/runs` model request. Status, server
configuration and OAuth authorization links/results use the same conversation.
`/mcp help` lists the operations. Enroll the actual WebUI actor in the Core
administrator configuration when privileged user commands are restricted.
OAuth browser approval remains with the user; do not paste access/refresh tokens.

## Network

Absent explicit network configuration, bind to loopback. Network access requires
native TLS, exact canonical Host/Origin and a configured identity service.
Authentication sessions and peer tokens remain backend-owned. Unknown routes and
all former static asset paths return 404.

Deploy the standalone dashboard against this API before upgrading an installation
that previously depended on embedded assets. Update the module path through its
configuration owner and use fresh host update admission before runtime replacement.
Do not remove retained history, credentials, approvals or execution contexts.

## Tests

```sh
npm test --prefix dashboard-api
node --import ./core/node_modules/tsx/dist/loader.mjs dashboard-api/test/host.mjs ./core
```

Frontend builds and browser tests belong to the WebUI repository.

# Outbound AgentLink over WebSocket

An agent can initiate a persistent WSS connection to the central dashboard. The
central instance sends scoped RPC requests and receives replies over that same
connection. The target needs outbound HTTPS access, not an inbound listening port,
NAT rule, Tailscale membership or a second agent runtime.

Direct AgentLink HTTPS remains supported. This transport is selected explicitly;
it does not automatically resend productive requests over another path.

## Central instance

Install the independently released backend overlay. Enable these startup plugins
in order, preserving other agent-specific modules:

```yaml
plugins:
  - /installed-overlay/credentials/index.mjs
  - /installed-overlay/workspace/index.mjs
  - /installed-overlay/agent-link/index.mjs
  - /installed-overlay/agent-link/relay.mjs
  - /installed-overlay/agent-hub/index.mjs
  - /installed-overlay/dashboard-api/index.mjs
```

`agent-link-relay.json`:

```json
{"origin":"https://dashboard.example.org"}
```

`agent-hub.json`:

```json
{"adapters":["hayate","hayate-wss"]}
```

The API-only dashboard gateway provides native TLS and the identity service as
usual. Add the identity plugin where authenticated network administration is
used. Deploy the independent WebUI with a verified HTTPS upstream to that API.
The frontend forwards only the fixed enrollment/leave paths and authenticated
WebSocket upgrade path, not arbitrary tunnels. Both the standalone frontend and
combined administration use the same relay service and protocol.

Public paths on the dashboard HTTPS origin:

- `POST /api/agent-link/v1/enroll`: one-use invitation exchange.
- `GET /api/agent-link/v1/connect`: authenticated WebSocket upgrade.
- `POST /api/agent-link/v1/leave`: authenticated target-initiated revocation.

Browser administration uses authenticated `/api/workspace/agent-relay` routes;
agent connections use separate scoped credentials, never browser cookies.

## Target agent

Enable `credentials/index.mjs`, `workspace/index.mjs` and
`agent-link/outbound.mjs`. No `agent-link/server.mjs` listener is required.

`agent-link-outbound.json`:

```json
{
  "relays":[{"origin":"https://dashboard.example.org"}],
  "capabilities":["projects","streams","messages","activity"],
  "projects":{},
  "shareStandalone":true
}
```

Local project mappings remain explicit. Empty mappings grant no access to local
projects; `shareStandalone` independently permits chats without a project. The
central invitation can reduce, but not expand, the target's capability list.
For private certificate authorities, an operator may configure a local `caFile`
on a relay entry. Certificate verification and hostname checks remain enabled.
`allowOperatorRelays:true` optionally permits operator-entered trusted HTTPS
origins without enumerating them; the default is the explicit relay allowlist.

Startup changes use the agent's normal configuration owner and fresh update
admission. Installing the overlay alone does not enable either side.

## Manual enrollment and approval

1. Centrally: **Agents → Invite outbound agent**. Choose a name and get a masked,
   single-use invitation, valid for five minutes.
2. On the target: **Agents → Connect this agent outbound**, or as administrator:
   `/agent-link-outbound enroll https://dashboard.example.org <invitation-code>`.
3. Centrally: refresh incoming connections, inspect identity and permissions, then
   choose **Approve and register**. Merely opening a socket does not register an
   agent or grant permission to execute work.
4. Use the registered agent through the normal AgentHub API and dashboard.

Headless central commands: `/agent-relay invite <name>`, `list`, `accept <id>` and
`reject <id>`. Target commands: `/agent-link-outbound status` and `disconnect`.
Codes must not appear in URLs or permanent browser storage. Permanent tokens stay
in backend vaults; relay state stores only token hashes.

## Failure and lifecycle behavior

- TLS must validate at both hops. Redirects, browser-cookie authentication and
  arbitrary proxy destinations are not supported.
- Ping/pong detects stale sessions; reconnect has bounded exponential backoff.
- An expired/revoked authorization stops reconnecting until operator action.
- Reconnect creates a new connection generation. Pending requests on a lost
  connection fail with an explicit unknown-outcome error; they are never replayed.
- Explicit message retry retains the original message UUID. Stream creation over
  WSS requires an idempotency UUID. Core ingress remains responsible for durable
  acceptance and deduplication, including after transport loss.
- Cancelling a wait does not cancel already accepted agent work. Target shutdown
  fences new input and drains entered work before releasing lifecycle ownership.
- Idle sockets do not block update admission. Enrollment, administration and RPC
  calls participate in foreground-work admission.
- Frames, pending requests, connections and response buffers are bounded. There
  is no interactive shell, generic HTTP forwarding or private host-control API.
- Removing the registration revokes the outbound authorization and closes the
  live socket. It does not delete histories or undo previously accepted work.

## Build and test

```sh
npm ci --prefix agent-link --include=dev --ignore-scripts
npm run build --prefix agent-link
node --test agent-link/test/*.test.mjs
```

The build packages the pinned `ws` implementation and its license under
`agent-link/vendor/` for standalone overlay installation. No runtime npm install
or new Core revision pin is required. Real Core-host tests additionally exercise
host ownership, immutable cwd, durable deduplication and idle update admission.

# Hayate-to-Hayate overlay connection

A small HTTPS adapter and target endpoint, independent of WebUI. No Core asset
pins, additional runtime or dependency framework. It uses the existing version-1
workspace/agent-hub services and Core foreground admission. Pi/Claude Code/Codex
can get separate adapters later; this implementation does not pretend to support them.

## Explicit setup

Keep the overlay checkout separate from Core. On each participating host install
Node >=22.19 and a compatible Core providing execution contexts, service lookup
and foreground work. These capabilities are checked during plugin activation.

For a target accepting requests, load in this order:

```yaml
plugins:
  - /opt/hayate-plugins/credentials/index.mjs
  - /opt/hayate-plugins/workspace/index.mjs
  - /opt/hayate-plugins/agent-link/index.mjs
  - /opt/hayate-plugins/agent-hub/index.mjs
  - /opt/hayate-plugins/agent-link/server.mjs
```

A client-only central host omits the final target-server entry. `agent-link/index`
registers the outbound adapter before agent-hub loads it. The server entry registers
a host-owned channel; it only listens when the host starts its channels and drains
accepted requests when the host stops them.

`<home>/agent-hub.json`:

```json
{ "adapters": ["hayate"] }
```

`<home>/agent-link.json` on a central/client host:

```json
{ "peers": [], "allowOperatorTargets": true }
```

A target adds `listen` to its file:

```json
{
  "peers": [],
  "listen": {
    "host": "127.0.0.1",
    "port": 3211,
    "origin": "https://target.example.org:3211",
    "keyFile": "/absolute/private/key.pem",
    "certFile": "/absolute/fullchain.pem",
    "projects": { "central-project-uuid": "existing-local-project-uuid" }
  }
}
```

The example binds only to loopback. DNS, certificates, firewall and any external
bind address are explicit operator choices, never changed by installation. Native
TLS is mandatory. Keys must be private regular files owned by the process user.
With `allowOperatorTargets: true`, the authenticated operator can register additional
target origins through the UI without editing deployment files. The default remains
allowlist-only; `peers` can still specify private CA trust per target. Both modes
accept canonical HTTPS origins only and verify certificates
against system trust; an optional per-peer `caFile` adds an explicit operator CA.
There is no `rejectUnauthorized:false` option or redirect following.

The project map is the complete set of target projects exposed by this endpoint.
It maps an origin-side project's ID to an existing target-side project. All paired
peers see only mapped projects, restricted further by their granted capability
names. There is no per-peer project selector yet: use separate endpoint/host trust
boundaries if peers must see different project sets. A peer cannot supply cwd or
clone paths; created streams use the target project's existing local directories.

## Pair and use

On the **target**, generate a five-minute, single-use code with
`/agent-hub pair https://central.example.org`
from an administrator TUI/messaging session, or with the WebUI registration-code
button. The slash command returns the target endpoint, code, expiry and optional
WebUI origin. It refuses to imply usable pairing if the target endpoint is not
installed. The WebUI address is guidance, not an automatic credential destination;
codes are never embedded in URLs. The code is temporary pairing authority, not a reusable password. Store
and transport it accordingly. Only its hash is persisted by the target.

On the **central** WebUI: Projects → workspace menu → Agents → Register an agent.
Choose adapter `hayate`, the allowlisted target HTTPS origin, its code and a display
name/color. The browser submits the code once; the returned peer token stays in the
server vault and is never returned to the browser. Open streams to view/send target
work. A project's dashboard also resolves the target mapping, lists local and
remote streams and offers the target in the shared composer. While visible, the
selected project's remote state refreshes every five seconds, with manual refresh
available. This is bounded read-only polling, not federated SSE or automatic
productive request retry. Unavailable/unshared/unsupported targets are displayed
explicitly; the composer never silently falls back to another agent.

Headless administrators can use the same services/commands:

```text
/agent-hub connect {"adapter":"hayate","endpoint":"https://target.example.org:3211","code":"<temporary-code>","name":"Target"}
/agent-hub request {"agentId":"<registration-id>","capability":"streams","input":{"action":"list"}}
/agent-hub sync <local-project-id>
/agent-hub remove <registration-id>
```

Only temporary pairing codes belong in the connect flow; never paste vault tokens
or passwords into a command/transcript. Shared settings use the explicit project
mapping. Project sync sends only ID/title/settings, not the central cwd. Individual
failures are returned to the caller. Target work still enters its normal workspace
channel, host queue, approvals, tool policy and durable reply delivery.

The protocol supports `projects` (list/resolve/apply), `streams` (list/create), `messages`
(read/send/mark-read) and `activity` (list), gated by the issued code's capabilities. Message
submission requires the original stable UUID on retries. The WebUI preserves an
unconfirmed remote send in session storage, without automatically resending it.
Creating a stream from the shared composer also uses a stable creation UUID; the
workspace stores/deduplicates it before any work is submitted. Targets advertise
`idempotent-stream-create` and `read-markers` in the mapping response. The UI only
offers these additions when advertised, so independently updated overlays do not
need an exact revision match. Mapping/stream failures do not retarget work.

## Revocation and failure handling

- The target stores only peer-token hashes; the client stores plaintext tokens only
  in its encrypted vault. Tokens expire after 30 days by default; target
  `listen.tokenLifetimeMs` may be explicitly set between one second and 365 days.
- Removing a Hayate registration first revokes the token on the target. If the
  target is unavailable, the local registration is retained for an explicit retry.
  Revocation is idempotent; it does not replay productive work.
- Target administrators can use `/agent-link list` and `/agent-link revoke <id>`
  without the central host. Revoked/expired tokens cannot submit further requests.
- A lost pairing response can leave an orphan target grant. List/revoke it on the
  target before pairing with a new code. Codes are not restored or silently reused.
- A lost productive response has unknown outcome. Read the target stream and retry
  only with the same message ID when appropriate. No automatic reconnect retry or
  assumption that an HTTP error means no work occurred.
- Target API requests reject browser Origin/Cookie headers, enforce canonical Host,
  JSON/body bounds and bounded concurrent pairing. It exposes no login/CORS or
  generic shell endpoint. TLS calls have absolute timeouts and no connection pool.

## Verification without live exposure

```sh
node --test agent-link/test/*.test.mjs
HARNESS_CORE_ROOT=/path/to/core node --import /path/to/core/node_modules/tsx/dist/loader.mjs --test agent-link/test/*.test.mjs
npm run test:browser --prefix webui
```

Temporary loopback certificates are explicitly trusted as test CAs, not bypassed.
Tests cover pairing replay, certificate rejection, allowlist/scope/project checks,
settings propagation, message/reply delivery, expiry/revocation and the actual Core
plugin/channel registration, deduplication and update admission. The Chromium test
registers a target through the authenticated central UI, sends remote work and
verifies target authorization is revoked when the registration is removed.

# Explicit authenticated HTTPS WebUI (development)

The optional `identity/` backend owns single-operator authentication independently
of WebUI. The WebUI owns TLS/HTTP projection, the login form and the secure cookie.
It does not store passwords, password hashes or bearer tokens in browser storage,
project state or transcripts. Neither package changes live networking automatically.
This separately installed overlay requires Core's foreground-work contract and
version-1 service registry. It checks those capabilities on activation; no exact
Core or overlay revision pin or inclusion in Core's release assets is required.

## Bootstrap locally, not through an agent conversation

In an operator terminal (password entry is hidden):

```sh
node /opt/hayate-plugins/identity/setup.mjs /absolute/agent-home admin
```

This creates a private `identity.json` with a salted scrypt password verifier.
The setup refuses to overwrite existing configuration. Never paste the password
into a chat, model tool, command argument, Git remote or shell history. The identity
plugin requires a mode-0600, operator-owned regular file, refusing symlinks and
hard links. Private host filesystem custody remains necessary; this is not an
isolation boundary against unrestricted tools running as the same OS user.

Load identity before the WebUI gateway starts:

```yaml
plugins:
  - /opt/hayate-plugins/identity/index.mjs
  # other headless backend plugins as needed
```

The current principal is deliberately `operator`: this is authenticated remote
access to an existing single-operator agent, **not multiuser hosting**. Login names
do not introduce separate permissions or identities. Legacy conversations, project
commands and secret entries retain their existing operator ownership.

## Configure TLS only after explicit operator approval

An operator must supply DNS, a valid certificate/private key, firewall/port routing
and an explicit network configuration. Development and installation do none of these.
Example `<home>/webui-network.json`:

```json
{
  "host": "0.0.0.0",
  "origin": "https://agent.example.org:3210",
  "keyFile": "/absolute/private/tls/key.pem",
  "certFile": "/absolute/tls/fullchain.pem"
}
```

The listener still uses `HAYATE_WEBUI_PORT` (default 3210). The bind host must be a
literal IP. `origin` must be a canonical HTTPS origin with no userinfo/path/query.
Use a certificate valid for that hostname and an operator-owned mode-0600 regular
private key. Symlink TLS files are refused: copy/atomically replace renewed PEMs
at the configured regular-file paths and restart through normal host admission.
TLS configuration is validated before presentation modules acquire resources.
No runtime ACME client, DNS changes, reverse-proxy trust or certificate-reload loop
is installed. An absent network file preserves the existing unauthenticated exact
`127.0.0.1` local-only listener. An invalid file, missing identity service or unsafe
TLS key **fails startup**, never falls back to anonymous network access.

Direct TLS is required; the application does not infer authentication, TLS, authority
or client IP from `Forwarded` / `X-Forwarded-*` headers. Keep public exposure disabled
until overlay compatibility, operator configuration and deployment checks have been reviewed.
Do not put a public HTTP-terminating proxy in front of legacy loopback mode.

## Security behavior

- Every API and SSE route is authenticated in network mode, including capability,
  directory, project, credential and agent endpoints. Only static login assets and
  `/api/auth` are public. Login/logout mutations still require exact Origin and
  the WebUI custom header. No CORS grants exist.
- Authority must exactly match the configured canonical origin. Cross-site fetch
  metadata is refused; arbitrary forwarded-user/proto headers have no authority.
- Password checks use scrypt and constant-time verifier comparison, with bounded
  concurrent derivations and bounded per-socket-IP rate-limit state. The supplied
  username has no effect on client rate limiting. Passwords are never logged.
- Sessions use random 256-bit opaque tokens, stored only as hashes server-side.
  Cookies are `__Host-` scoped with `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict`, `Path=/`
  and expiry. They are audience-bound to the canonical HTTPS origin. The browser
  cannot retrieve tokens through JavaScript or a JSON authentication response.
- Default idle lifetime is one hour; `sessionLifetimeMs` in `identity.json` can be
  explicitly configured between one second and 24 hours. `POST /api/auth/renew`
  extends a valid session and refreshes its secure cookie. The compatible WebUI
  renews on trusted, visible user interaction at most once a minute; polling and
  SSE do not extend idle time. Very short configured lifetimes below that cadence
  can still expire during use.
- Session hashes and expiries persist in private `<home>/identity/account.json`
  and survive regular backend restarts. Existing memory-only sessions need one
  new login after upgrading. Logout durably revokes the token before expiring the
  cookie and clearing this application's pending browser drafts.
- Revocation/expiry prevents further SSE data immediately at projection time and
  closes idle streams within the two-second server maintenance interval. HTTP
  mutation body parsing rechecks authentication after upload. The UI locks when
  expiry is detected and never automatically retries productive submissions.
- Identity password derivations and session writes reserve host foreground
  admission and are drained on stop. Stopped instances reject authentication;
  unexpired persisted sessions remain valid on the next activation.

For routine changes use **Account settings** in the sidebar: choose login name and
optional new password, confirm the current password and save. Changes persist in
private `<home>/identity/account.json`, take precedence over the installation's
bootstrap `identity.json`, and revoke all existing sessions. The operator principal
and ownership of projects/credentials do not change when the login name changes.
Changes affect this dashboard instance, not accounts on paired targets. No passwords
enter chat, model tools, browser storage or API responses. Write failures retain the
prior credentials and live sessions.

Local recovery after a forgotten password is an operator-controlled maintenance
operation: stop normally, replace private bootstrap configuration, remove/reset the
private account override intentionally and restart. There is no anonymous recovery
API or password reset through a chat command. Kubernetes init must restore private
mode on retained `identity/account.json` if fsGroup broadens it at mount time.

# Dispatcher parent decisions

Requires a compatible Core with `Dispatcher.decide` and the durable execution
receipt contracts. The plugin remains an adapter; it does not edit the ledger or
override completion, recovery, approval or task-authority policy.

Tool: `plugin_dispatch({action: "decide", id, requestId, decision})`.
Command (host-authenticated admin): `/dispatch decide <id> <requestId> <text>`.
The parent is always the trusted session context, never a tool argument. Nested
`dispatch:` and `subagent:` sessions are rejected through both surfaces.

Acceptance returns `recorded: true` and a receipt with `state: pending|applied`.
Pending means not delivered to a strategy boundary yet. Applied means consumed
by trusted strategy code, not acceptance of the requested deviation or proof of
completion. Original mandate/constraints and independent evidence checks remain
binding. See Core `docs/dispatcher.md` for boundary fencing and supported strategies.

Read exact retained receipts with status `id` plus `field: decisions`; use
`charOffset` for 8,000-character pages. Ordinary status and `/dispatch status`
show bounded receipt summaries. An identical retry reuses its original receipt;
a conflicting requestId is rejected. Preserve command whitespace when retrying:
the text after the id/requestId separator is kept verbatim, including newlines.

Core bounds: requestId 1–128 ASCII alphanumerics/`._:-` starting alphanumeric;
nonblank decision text at most 4,000 UTF-8 bytes; at most 32 receipts and 16,000
UTF-8 bytes of JSON decision input per execution. Cancelled/completed/foreign
or parent-stopped tasks reject writes. Audits are retained through reload.

Resume does not accept task text: use decide for steering, answer for an existing
pending question, and resume only for an otherwise-resolvable pause.

Build against Core using an explicit local materialization lock for development.
The adapter also typechecks against older Core contracts through an optional
capability projection, but never emulates a missing decision API. Production needs a new immutable plugins revision/hash lock in Core.
New adapters fail explicitly for decide on older running hosts; older adapters do
not expose decide. Source builds do not activate changes: external authorized
rollout/restart is required. No live execution/ledger edits are part of this change.

# Memory consolidation policy plugin

`src/memory-consolidation.mjs` implements a bounded, persistent consolidation
orchestrator. Core PR #315 supplies the trusted host adapter (merged as
`66d4882b207440dd9a772570619615f66ed8ab2f`). A host must run that revision or newer
and configure `memory.consolidation` to register service version 1 before loading
this module. Installing this source alone does not activate consolidation.

Service contract:
- `tier`: explicit `frontier` (2 hours) or `local` (12 hours).
- `capture(turn)` / `recall(sessionKey, text)`: existing memory service delegation.
- `put({sessionKey}, entry)`: current memory provider, preserving session isolation.
- `summarize({sessionKey, requestId, sources, instruction})`: isolated, no-tool,
  low-cost model execution. The adapter owns model configuration, cancellation,
  bounded execution, authorization and durable dispatcher dedup by requestId if
  implemented via the dispatcher. No additional authority is inferred from data.
- Optional `log(message)`.

The module registers `consolidating` as a memory orchestrator. Host configuration
must select it explicitly. Timers use foreground admission and drain on plugin
shutdown. A one-minute poll processes at most one conversation batch of 16 sources;
64 pending sources per conversation and 1000 conversations are bounded.
Eligible conversations are ordered by oldest attempt. Failures retain their batch
and receive a persisted exponential cooldown (one minute up to one hour), so a
broken model/provider request cannot monopolize subsequent ticks. Remaining
backlog after a successful batch stays immediately due instead of waiting another
full interval. Budgets
fail explicitly rather than discarding queued raw information. They are not a
promise that an overloaded/offline worker can meet the cadence.

Captured raw outcomes remain in the normal memory provider. The plugin retains a
private derived work queue and isolates conversation scopes. Successful summaries
are stored as reported lessons with input IDs recorded as provenance text, never
as independent verification. Provider `links` are reserved for actual memory-entry
IDs and remain empty; message IDs must not be passed as memory links. They do not expire automatically. Pending work and generated output
survive restart; provider-write retries reuse the exact same key and payload.
A crash before the generated result is persisted can repeat a model call, so the
host adapter should deduplicate requestId if it uses durable workers. No source
instructions are executed. Prompt instructions alone do not guarantee semantic
summary quality; a no-tool runtime is required in the host adapter.

This slice establishes tested policy and persistence only. Core adapter and model routing are supplied by Core PR #315. The combined
plugin/host/provider test passes against that revision using a fake model runtime;
live activation and real-model acceptance remain delivery dependencies.

Run the combined check with:

```
HARNESS_CORE_ROOT=/path/to/core node --import /path/to/core/node_modules/tsx/dist/loader.mjs --test test/memory-consolidation*.test.mjs
```

# Project workspace implementation plan

## Requirements and boundaries

1. Real execution contexts: pick allowed server directories and Git checkouts;
   persist a primary cwd plus explicit additional roots. Never use process.chdir.
   Runtime tools, persona, plugin tools, commands, review policies and delegated
   workers must resolve the same immutable stream context. Changing a project's
   settings affects new streams, not already-authorized active work.
2. Secret integrations: browser write-only credential submission, no transcript,
   SSE, export or localStorage secret values. Private encrypted local vault;
   explicit OpenBao KV and external password-manager providers. Server keeps
   provider trust/address/config; HTTP input cannot run arbitrary secret commands.
3. Projects: nested grouping, multiple directories/repositories/streams, per-agent
   membership, archive/soft-delete, conversion and drag/drop of sessions. Existing
   transcript store migrates additively, without destructive history changes.
4. Notifications: persisted terminal turn revisions + per-principal read markers;
   completion/failure points in collapsed project/session trees, no polling model.
5. Dashboard: project overview and aggregated activity, safe statuses, centered
   next-step composer, explicit stream target and stable task ownership.
6. Federation: expiring, single-use pairing generated by the target via WebUI or
   privileged startup-plugin command; validate over authenticated HTTPS, retain
   scoped peer tokens only in encrypted server vault. Central browser never sees
   peer tokens. Per-agent names/colors and connection states; project fan-out must
   expose partial failures and never retry unknown productive submissions blindly.
7. Network: canonical origin + exact Host checks, HTTPS, scrypt operator login,
   HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite session cookies, expiry/revocation, same-origin mutation
   checks, principal-bound project/session ownership and SSE authorization.
   No permissive CORS, trusted-forwarded-header inference or anonymous LAN mode.

## Vertical slices and acceptance

A. Generic Core execution-context capability + plugin-owned projects/pickers:
   verify two simultaneous directories, actual tools and formal review binding,
   delegated inheritance, persistence/restart and refusal to retarget a used stream.
B. Project UI: expandable tree, menus, + stream, dashboard, activity/unread,
   archive/delete/convert/move; Chromium keyboard/mobile/scroll regressions.
C. Secrets and Git providers: secure file/key handling, AEAD, origin-bound remote
   calls with redirects refused, provider adapters, no secret in API/event history.
D. Network identity: login/logout/expiry, authority mapping and per-principal
   isolation; test every HTTP/SSE route, CSRF/rebinding, TLS startup requirements.
E. Multi-agent: consume/replay/expiry tests, scoped token revocation, central SSE,

F. Final gates: existing plugin tests, new backend/security/Core integration,

# Local Slack gateway: DMs, engaged channel threads and files

This is an optional trusted GatewayModule v1, not a bundled Core channel. It uses
Node's native fetch/WebSocket and `node:crypto`, with no package installation at
runtime. Use Node 24 (the tested runtime). One workspace per process, discovered
from the bot token. DMs work without mentions and share a stable per-DM session.
In public/private channels, an explicit mention (whether delivered as `app_mention`
or as a normal `message` event containing the bot mention) engages a thread; subsequent
messages in that thread continue without another mention, including after restart.
Other channel traffic is ignored by default. Per-channel access, activation and reply
location can be configured through the shared conversation-policy contract below.
Thread membership is atomically persisted without
message contents. A channel allowlist is optional, not required for connection.
Inbound files and supported images use Core's session-bound attachment contract v1.
History import, group-DM conversation handling, reactions and interactive approvals
are not implemented. Core's native messaging tool supports images/binary uploads
with an optional caption, new channel posts, DMs and thread replies.

## 1. Prepare the Slack app (administrator)

1. Create an internal Slack app from `examples/slack-app-manifest.json` in the
   intended test workspace. The manifest requests `app_mentions:read`,
   `chat:write`, `files:read`, `im:history`, `channels:history`, `groups:history`,
   `channels:read` and `groups:read`. The last two permit joined-channel discovery.
   Events are `app_mention`, `message.im`, `message.channels` and `message.groups`.
   Message/history scopes are required to receive DM and channel-thread events;
   the adapter does not call history APIs or import channel archives. Socket Mode
   needs no public Request URL.
2. Under Basic Information → App-Level Tokens generate an app token with
   `connections:write`. This app-level scope is separate from bot OAuth scopes;
   it is not silently granted by the manifest.
3. Install the app into that workspace and obtain its bot OAuth token. Reinstall
   after any future scope change. Invite the bot into the isolated test channel.
4. No workspace or channel IDs are required for normal setup: `auth.test` supplies
   the workspace and bot identity, and events supply channel/thread IDs. Optionally
   restrict the workspace or channels as described below. Slack administrative
   status does not grant Hayate administrator rights.

The manifest includes `files:write` for the native file-send path. Existing installs
need reinstalling only if that scope is missing; never assume a checked-in manifest
changed the scopes of an already issued token. No slash-command or interactive-event permissions are requested. DM and channel
message scopes are explicitly paired with their corresponding events. App-level `connections:write` is generated separately, not a bot scope.

The manifest disables token rotation for this minimal internal app. If rotation
is required by policy, implement refresh support before using this adapter.
Do not publish this Socket Mode app to the Marketplace.

## 2. Provision configuration and install the module

Through the existing secret/deployment process, provide these environment values
to the agent process (never commit the actual values):

- `SLACK_APP_TOKEN`: app-level token, normally `xapp-…`.
- `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`: bot OAuth token, normally `xoxb-…`.
These **two tokens are the only required Slack settings**. With neither token
set, the factory returns unconfigured; with only one, it fails closed.

Optional restrictions (leave unset for normal setup):

- `SLACK_TEAM_ID`: pin the discovered workspace to this ID (`T…`); mismatch fails.
- `SLACK_CHANNEL_IDS`: comma-separated channel allowlist (`C…` / `G…`), no wildcard.
  When unset, mentions can be handled in any channel accessible to the bot.

IDs are stable identifiers, not display names. Restricting channels is an operator
policy choice, not a Slack authentication requirement. Environment updates require the normal authorized process rollout;
plugin reload cannot replace a process environment. Tokens are not read from chat
messages or included in error messages.

**Dependency / deployment order:** first deliver the Core change providing
`GatewayFactoryContext.inboundAttachments = 1`, durable session-bound inbound
references and runtime image plumbing (Core PR #282, merge
`cbec53bfa46bda14b17f162ad231c5042e4daba4`).
The configured factory refuses older hosts instead of silently dropping images.
Pin the reviewed Core and plugin commits in the actual deployment; a branch name
is not a release or evidence of activation.

Copy the reviewed **exact** `src/slack-gateway.mjs`, `src/slack-files.mjs`,
`src/slack-upload.mjs`, `src/slack-threads.mjs` and `src/conversation-policy.mjs` from
the same pinned plugin commit into a new versioned directory, for example:

```
<home>/plugins/slack/<commit>/slack-gateway.mjs
<home>/plugins/slack/<commit>/slack-files.mjs
<home>/plugins/slack/<commit>/slack-upload.mjs
<home>/plugins/slack/<commit>/slack-threads.mjs
<home>/plugins/slack/<commit>/conversation-policy.mjs
```

Use normal artifact/GitOps provisioning; no runtime downloads or mutable shared
imports. This standalone `.mjs` is not a materialized TypeScript builtin and must
not be added blindly to Core's `plugins.lock.json` or generated `builtin-plugins`.

An authorized operator then selects the installed module:

```
/gateway-plugin use slack plugins/slack/<commit>/slack-gateway.mjs
/gateway-plugin status
```

The existing manager supports arbitrary non-reserved gateway IDs including
`slack`; desired selection is persisted under `gatewayPlugins`. Activation waits
for the existing safe idle boundary. `create()` performs no network operations;
`start()` checks the token's workspace with `auth.test` before opening the socket.
The adapter does not change the default home destination or operator/admin list.
If private administrative access is required, configure the explicit sender ID
`slack:<workspace-id>:<user-id>` through the existing operator configuration;
do not broaden an existing admin list merely to test chat delivery.

## Channel policy: defaults, access and replies

Use the shared Core `gateways.overrides.slack.conversation` contract, not Slack
scopes or prompt prose as a substitute for admission policy:

```yaml
gateways:
  overrides:
    slack:
      conversation:
        allowedChannels: "*"
        defaults:
          users: "*"
          activation: threads
          replyLocation: thread
        channels:
          C_PRIVATE_OPERATOR:
            activation: open
            replyLocation: channel
          C_RESTRICTED:
            users: [U_OPERATOR_ID]
            activation: mentions
```

`users: "*"` permits all human users; `users: []` denies all. Unknown/new channels
inherit the defaults. Channel overrides change only the named fields.
`activation` is `mentions` (mention every time), `threads` (mention to engage,
then thread follow-ups), `open` (consider unaddressed input but allow NO_REPLY),
or `disabled`. `replyLocation` is `thread` or `channel`; channel-level replies
share a stable channel conversation. DMs still require no mention but enforce
access restrictions. User checks happen before thread lookup or attachment
download. Own/bot messages and edits cannot cause loops. This grants no admin
or approver rights and does not auto-join Slack channels. The legacy
`SLACK_CHANNEL_IDS` allowlist, if set, remains an additional hard restriction.

An authenticated Core administrator can use `/conversation-policy defaults slack
<JSON>`, `/conversation-policy channel slack <ID> <JSON>`, and
`/conversation-policy channels slack <"*" or JSON ID array>` for persistent live
changes. Local/installation/drop-in files use the ordinary restart/activation
lifecycle. New restrictive policy on an older unsupported adapter fails closed.

## 3. Verify before admitting ordinary use

- Mention the bot in a channel it has joined (and, if configured, allowed by the optional restriction): the answer must be in that message's
  thread. An explicit mention in the thread continues that same session.
- Verify no response to bot messages, edited messages, unmentioned messages or
  channels outside an explicitly configured allowlist. Without an allowlist, verify
  a second joined channel works without additional configuration. Session keys include workspace, channel and
  exact string thread timestamp. Input IDs use workspace/channel/message timestamp. This also deduplicates app_mention and
  message events for the same message through Core's durable inbox, even when
  Slack assigns different event IDs. Socket envelopes are acknowledged individually.
- Core's `deliverInbound` promise must represent **durable** inbox acceptance;
  only then is the Socket Mode envelope acknowledged. If storage fails, no ACK
  is sent; disconnect permits upstream redelivery. Redelivery deduplication is
  Core-owned, not an in-memory plugin claim of exactly-once processing.
- Verify reconnect, process restart and persisted module selection in the actual
  deployment. The local fake tests do not prove those live properties.
- Replace with another version and check that the old receiver stops first.
  The factory declares `updateAdmission: "foreground-owned"`: creation is inert,
  reconnects belong to the stopped channel, and shutdown synchronously fences
  new ingress and outbound sends. Shutdown waits for the socket to close and for
  accepted ingress, outbound response bodies and complete upload/persistence
  operations to settle. Timeout is an error, never a claim of safe replacement.
  Failed delivery outcomes still reach Core's durable outbox; shutdown does not
  replay them or claim unknown external effects succeeded. A failed start can be followed by the manager's
  existing stop/rollback sequence. Versioned paths avoid the ESM cache trap.

## Attachment storage and trust boundary

Up to four inbound files, 10 MiB each and 20 MiB total per message. Files are
stored below `<home>/attachments/<SHA256(sessionKey)>/<SHA256(bytes)>`, synced to
disk before durable inbox acceptance and reverified before prompting. A foreign
session cannot relabel a reference to read another session's directory. Root and
parent directories are trusted operator-owned storage, not a sandbox against a
malicious local process with access to the agent home. Core uses no-follow regular
file opens and bounded reads. Image signatures select PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP; this is
not a complete image decoder or malware scanner. The provider may reject malformed
images. A model without image capability fails explicitly. Other binaries are
provided as local file references, not automatically parsed.

Files in an admitted event are handled, including attachment-only messages.
Missing URL/size metadata is resolved with bounded authenticated `files.info` by
exact file ID before download; missing/unavailable metadata fails visibly.
A rejected user or channel cannot trigger file lookups/downloads. Slack file
visibility/event shape must still be verified with the installed app. Downloads reject redirects, non-HTTPS and hosts other than
`files.slack.com`; tokens must never follow an external redirect.

No automatic blob garbage collection is implemented. Preserve files for queued
inputs and runtime references; monitor persistent-volume capacity and apply an
operator-managed retention policy only after proving references are no longer
needed. This is not unlimited archival storage.

## 4. Outbound behavior and operational limits

### Native discovery and operator-authorized sends

On Core versions exposing `plugin_message`, active Slack availability and destination
format are supplied as host facts on every turn, including conversations on Matrix,
API or another gateway. `plugin_message status` inspects live gateways;
`destinations` with `gateway: "slack"` pages joined public/private channels using
`users.conversations`. It never lists all workspace channels or joins channels.
Slack does not include `is_member` on that endpoint: do not filter away real
memberships based on the absent field. Names are untrusted data; use exact target
IDs and follow `nextCursor`. This read-only listing requires `channels:read` and
`groups:read`; missing scopes fail explicitly without hiding working send support.
Existing installations that already grant these scopes need no Slack reinstall.

`plugin_message send` accepts `gateway`, `target`, `text` and a stable `requestId`.
For a file, supply `file: {path, name?}` and optional caption in `text`. The path
must be a regular current-workspace file or an inbound blob owned by this
conversation. Core snapshots at most 10 MiB, validates scope/name/hash and passes
a host-bound attachment to Slack; no arbitrary file paths cross the adapter API.
The external-upload API supports new channel posts, DMs and exact thread replies.
The adapter verifies bytes and persists allocation/transfer/completion state;
unknown effects are never blindly replayed. `files` capability is advertised only
on hosts with the required outbound attachment contract.
Omit `thread` for a new channel post (or DM); provide the exact timestamp for a
thread reply. Membership and discovery grant no permission: the operator's current
mandate still authorizes the destination and message. The tool stores no-replay
receipts; retries with the same request return the retained outcome, and uncertain
sends require reconciliation. Never work around tool availability by retrieving
credentials or invoking a shell HTTP client. On older Core, automatic replies
work, but the model-visible discovery/send tool is unavailable until Core rollout.

Every logical text reply uses one `chat.postMessage` call, with `thread_ts` only
when replying in a thread, link/media
unfurling disabled, and a deterministic UUID derived from Core delivery ID plus
workspace/channel/thread. Do not interpret `client_msg_id` as a proven Slack
exactly-once guarantee. When Core supplies no delivery ID there is no such hint.

HTTP 429 records the method's `Retry-After` cooldown (integer seconds); calls
before it expires fail locally without a request. Missing/invalid headers use
60 seconds, zero uses one second. Slack logical `ratelimited` errors also use
60 seconds. This avoids sleeping in an active send or internally replaying it.
Core retains its normal outbox retry schedule; `retryAt` on the error is diagnostic
metadata, not a new Core scheduling contract. Cooldowns are process-local and
reset on restart. They are conservative per method, not a full workspace quota
scheduler.

Network failures, malformed replies and 5xx after a post are marked ambiguous.
The adapter performs **no internal resend**. Core may retry the outbox entry using
the same delivery ID; duplicate Slack posts remain possible after ambiguous
outcomes. Audit the thread before manual replay. No exactly-once claim is made.

Known Slack API error codes are reported without response payloads or tokens.
Permission/configuration errors propagate to Core; this standalone plugin has no
shared `PermanentDeliveryError` constructor, so such entries are not automatically
parked. Correct the app membership/scopes or use the existing authorized outbox
reconciliation path. Never silently acknowledge a failed outbound delivery.

Replies above 39,000 Unicode code points are rejected before posting (Slack
truncates above 40,000). This initial adapter does not split replies: chunking
without persisted per-chunk identities would introduce partial-delivery replays.
Do not use it for oversized reports until a tested durable chunking/file policy
is supplied. Slack's recommendation remains much shorter messages (~4,000).

## 5. Disable / rollback

```
/gateway-plugin disable slack
/gateway-plugin status
```

Restore by selecting the previous immutable module path. Do not use `baseline
slack`: Slack has no bundled baseline. Revoke the tokens only after stopping the
receiver, unless urgent credential containment requires immediate revocation.
Keep secrets out of logs, commits and example configuration.

```
node --test test/slack*.test.mjs
node --check src/slack-gateway.mjs
```

No Slack installation, token authentication, live acceptance test or activation
is implied by these checks. References: Slack Socket Mode documentation at
https://docs.slack.dev/apis/events-api/using-socket-mode/ and chat.postMessage at

# Headless workspace plugins and optional WebUI

This is a separately installed agent overlay, not part of the Core distribution.
It requires compatible Core execution-context, version-1 service-registry and
foreground-work contracts, checked when plugins activate. It does not require Core
to pin or package an exact overlay revision. Older hosts without these contracts
are unsupported; do not overwrite managed Core files to install it.

## Ownership

| Package | Responsibilities | Browser required? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `workspace/` | Projects, subprojects, immutable stream execution directories, organization, settings inheritance, persistent messages and unread revisions | No |
| `credentials/` | Write-only submissions, encrypted local vault, optional OpenBao KV-v2, trusted secret-provider service adapters | No |
| `git-catalog/` | Configured Forgejo/GitHub organization/repository inventory and local-checkout mappings | No |
| `agent-link/` | Explicitly configured HTTPS Hayate adapter and headless target endpoint | No |
| `agent-hub/` | Agent identities/presentation, one-use target codes, credential references and adapter-based requests/project synchronization | No |
| `identity/` | Single-operator scrypt authentication, audience-bound sessions and revocation | No |
| `dashboard-api/` | Authenticated HTTP/SSE projection of backend services and retained conversations; no browser assets | Yes |

Core owns transport-neutral execution-context binding and versioned in-process
service discovery. It does not own project records, vault implementations, HTTP
routes or federation policy. Model runtime, persona resources, tools, policy hooks,
formal review adapters and host-owned worker descendants resolve the stream's cwd.
Moving a stream in the project tree is organization only and never retargets execution.

Services are trusted in-process capabilities, not sandbox boundaries. `operator`
is the current single-operator principal shared with admin commands. Multiuser hosting is not implemented. [Explicit authenticated HTTPS](authenticated-webui.md)
is now available in development via the separate identity plugin and operator-owned
TLS configuration; it preserves the existing operator principal. Absent explicit
configuration, the WebUI remains exact-loopback only. Do not expose legacy mode
with a public proxy; no forwarded-header trust is inferred.

## Installation layout

Keep this overlay checkout (the package directories and `shared/`) together in a
trusted, operator-owned location, separate from Core's release directory. Update it
independently through the normal stop/update/restart workflow. Node must be at least
22.19; plugin API and service contracts are version 1. Features check the actual host
capabilities instead of requiring a matching Core Git revision. Once those contracts
are in a released Core version, document that minimum version here; do not invent a
minimum release number for the currently unreleased contracts.

Enable ESM entry points explicitly using Core's `plugins` configuration:

```yaml
plugins:
  - /opt/hayate-plugins/credentials/index.mjs
  - /opt/hayate-plugins/workspace/index.mjs
  - /opt/hayate-plugins/git-catalog/index.mjs
  - /opt/hayate-plugins/agent-hub/index.mjs
```

The last two entries are optional. Configure any `secret-provider-<name>` or
`agent-adapter-<name>` version-1 service before its consumer. Backend packages have
no browser dependencies; install/build WebUI separately as documented in its README.
Existing standalone chats remain available using the Projects/Chats toggle and
nonempty histories attach automatically under Existing chats. Project moves and
conversion preserve the original `webui:<id>` runtime key and original transcript;
workspace submission delegates back to that original gateway. No model history is
copied or reset, and the host context is never retargeted by project organization.

Configuration files in the agent home:

- `workspace.json`: optional `{ "roots": ["/srv/work"] }`; defaults to the host cwd.
  Picker and project creation enforce realpath containment, including symlinks.
- `credentials.json`: optional `{ "provider": "local" }` (default), or provider
  `openbao` with `address` (canonical HTTPS origin), `mount`, `prefix` and `tokenFile`.
  Other names resolve `secret-provider-<name>` implementations.
- `git-catalog.json`: required when enabling Git inventory; example below.
- `agent-hub.json`: optional `{ "adapters": [] }`; configured adapter names resolve
  trusted `agent-adapter-<name>` implementations.

```json
{
  "providers": [{
    "id": "company",
    "kind": "forgejo",
    "origin": "https://git.example.org",
    "credential": "vault-entry-id",
    "checkouts": { "team/application": "/srv/work/application" }
  }]
}
```

Git inventory is read-only. Repositories without an operator-configured local
checkout are displayed but cannot become execution contexts. Automatic clone,
credential injection into Git subprocesses, arbitrary password-manager commands
and remote write operations are deliberately absent. GitHub's API origin should
be `https://api.github.com`.

## Headless operation

Admin commands work without installing WebUI:

```text
/workspace project {"title":"Application","cwd":"/srv/work/application"}
/workspace stream {"projectId":"<project-id>","title":"Investigate"}
/workspace send {"streamId":"<stream-id>","id":"<stable-message-id>","text":"Inspect the checkout"}
/git-catalog providers
/git-catalog orgs company
/git-catalog repos company team
```

`workspace`, `credentials` and `agent-hub` also register version-1 services for trusted
frontends/integrations. Secrets are consumed only through backend `withSecret`
callbacks. Listing/UI/commands return metadata, never plaintext. Local encryption
protects files at rest, not against the same OS user or unrestricted agent shell
access. Restrict host filesystem/tool permissions accordingly.

[Hayate-to-Hayate connectivity](agent-link.md) is implemented as a separately
configured HTTPS adapter/endpoint. Pi, Claude Code and Codex remain future adapters.
Codes are
hashed in state and consumed atomically once. Adapters must validate target identity,
request scope and HTTPS before returning server-held tokens. Project synchronization
is explicit and returns per-agent failures; productive requests are not silently
retried. External-agent support should implement these adapters, not fork the UI.

## Verification

```sh
node --test workspace/test/*.test.mjs credentials/test/*.test.mjs git-catalog/test/*.test.mjs agent-hub/test/*.test.mjs identity/test/*.test.mjs agent-link/test/*.test.mjs
node --import ../core/node_modules/tsx/dist/loader.mjs workspace/test/host.mjs ../core
npm ci --prefix webui --include=dev
npm run build --prefix webui
npm test --prefix webui
npm run test:browser --prefix webui
npm test --prefix dashboard-api
# Frontend/browser tests run in the separate harness/webui repository.
```

The real-host headless test covers channel/service registration, commands, context
binding, durable replies, retry deduplication and update admission without an HTTP
server. Core's execution-context runtime test exercises actual PI bash/plugin tools
concurrently in two directories and a worker-inherited directory. The review adapter tests also run the real formal-review service against two
independent Git changesets while the startup cwd is not a repository. Immutable
compatibility with the first Core release providing the required contracts remains
to be verified. Overlay updates do not require changing Core's asset/source locks.

No additional repository or frontend framework is needed for this separation.
A later repository extraction must preserve these service contracts and version
compatibility rather than move domain logic back into the browser.
